lesson.title: Traceroute: Mapping a Path One Hop at a Time
lesson.summary: Traceroute discovers the sequence of routers between a source and a destination by deliberately sending probes that expire one hop further each time, reading the ICMP time exceeded message each expiry triggers.
lesson.body:
Ping tells you whether a destination answers, but it says nothing about the path packets took to get there. Traceroute answers that question, and it does so with a clever reuse of a mechanism that exists for an entirely different reason: the time to live field in the IP header.

Every IP packet carries a time to live counter that each router decrements by one as the packet passes through. This exists to stop packets from circulating forever if a routing loop ever forms: once the counter reaches zero, the router holding it discards the packet instead of forwarding it, and, as covered in the ICMP chapter, sends back an ICMP time exceeded message, type 11, to the original sender. Traceroute turns this failure signal into a mapping tool. It sends a first probe with the time to live deliberately set to 1. The very first router on the path decrements that value to zero, drops the probe, and reports back with a time exceeded message, revealing its own address as the first hop. Traceroute then sends a probe with time to live set to 2, which survives the first router but expires at the second, revealing the second hop. It keeps incrementing the time to live by one and sending a new probe for each value, and each router along the way, in turn, becomes the one that lets the counter hit zero and has to report back.

Imagine a path from a home network through an ISP router, then a regional router, then finally to a web server three hops away. Traceroute's probe with time to live 1 expires at the ISP router, revealing its address and the round trip time to reach it. The probe with time to live 2 expires at the regional router, revealing that address. The probe with time to live 3 finally survives long enough to reach the web server itself. Because that server is the actual destination rather than an intermediate hop, it does not send a time exceeded message. Traditional Unix traceroute exploits this by sending its probes as UDP packets aimed at an unusual, unlikely to be open port, so the destination responds with an ICMP destination unreachable, port unreachable message instead, which traceroute recognizes as the signal that it has reached the end of the path. Windows tracert instead sends ICMP echo requests as its probes, so the final hop answers with an ordinary echo reply.

Real traceroute output often shows gaps, printed as asterisks instead of an address and time. This does not always mean a router is down. Some routers are configured to rate limit or simply not generate ICMP time exceeded messages at all, so they show up as silent hops even though packets are passing through them successfully on their way to a destination that does respond. Reading a traceroute well means treating the list of hops it reveals as a genuine snapshot of the path, while remembering that a missing hop is often a router choosing not to answer rather than a break in the path itself.
